The named failure most managers actually commit is the first, not harshness.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a well-liked employee is quietly underperforming is scored on delivering the specific correction, since softening it to protect the relationship is the graded mistake.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: A business owned and run by two or more people who share profits and liabilities.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership law sets how partners share profits, decide, and bear business debts.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: The identity and reputation a person projects through their online presence.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal social media brand can boost or damage credibility.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Gable's strongest of four ways to answer someone's good news, formed by crossing active with passive and constructive with destructive: responding actively and constructively means asking questions that let the person relive the event, while passive-constructive is a flat nice job, active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive changes the subject. Only the first strengthens the relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays on recognizing a team member's contribution are scored on a specific, curious response in the moment rather than a generic congratulation or a deferred award.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: Makes an employer vicariously liable for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment even though the employer itself did nothing careless. A minor deviation from the route or task — a detour — stays inside that scope, while a substantial personal errand — a frolic — falls outside it, and a genuine independent contractor generally does not trigger the doctrine at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Agency roleplays about a delivery driver's crash ask whether the company pays, and the frolic-versus-detour line decides it.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: A gesture carrying a fixed verbal translation that works with no speech at all - a thumbs-up, a head shake, the finger-and-thumb ring - which is precisely what separates it from an illustrator, a gesture that means nothing apart from the words it accompanies, such as sketching a package's size in the air. Because the translation is assigned by culture rather than by resemblance, this type can invert across a border: the same ring means money in Japan and is obscene in Brazil.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay that has you demonstrate a product to a foreign buyer is scored on choosing gestures whose meaning does not flip, and exam items ask which gesture type still communicates when used silently.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Letting one strong impression, often a single outstanding trait, lift every unrelated rating for the same person; its inverse, the horns effect, drags them all down from one bad impression. In an appraisal it shows up as suspiciously uniform scores across dimensions that ought to vary, and the standard counter is rating every employee on one dimension at a time before moving to the next.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows an evaluation form with identical scores in every category is testing this, and an HR roleplay on fixing a review process is scored on the dimension-by-dimension fix.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: Binds a principal to a deal because the principal's own words or conduct led a third party to believe reasonably that the agent was authorized, even though no actual authority — express or implied — was ever granted. The manifestation must trace back to the principal, not to the agent's own claims, which is why an agent who simply asserts power creates none.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a terminated sales rep still carries company cards and signs an order tests this against actual authority.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of whether people define themselves as 'I' or as part of a permanent in-group: the United States scores about 91, the highest of the fifty-plus countries surveyed, and Guatemala about 6. It answers a different question than power distance, which measures tolerance of unequal authority, and a country can be strongly collectivist while low in power distance. The communication consequence differs accordingly - a high score licenses naming one person's contribution and negotiating one-to-one, a low score requires the group to settle a position before any single voice states it.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why singling out one employee for praise backfired with an overseas team is scored on this dimension, not on generic 'cultural differences.'

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: Deci and Ryan's account of motivation as three psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — plus a continuum running from purely external regulation through introjected and identified regulation to fully internalized motivation. Motivation is therefore a location on that continuum rather than an amount, and only the internalized end keeps working once the supervisor stops watching.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why a bonus program stopped producing results, or a roleplay on motivating a team without extra budget, is scored on giving choice, competence feedback and belonging instead of raising the payout.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: The charter filed with the secretary of state that brings a corporation into legal existence, stating its name, registered agent, purpose and the number of authorized shares, and amendable only by shareholder vote plus another state filing. Bylaws are the separate internal rulebook — meetings, officers, quorum, notice — adopted by the board, never filed publicly, and changed without any state involvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A venture roleplay asks which document has to change before more shares can be issued to a new investor.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: A short opening section of a report that distills key findings and recommendations.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward a crisp, decision-ready summary.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: Damping an emotion after it has already arrived by hiding its outward signs, rather than changing the interpretation that produced it. Because it is applied late, it leaves the physiological arousal fully intact, raises blood pressure in the person watching as well, and measurably impairs memory for what was said during the episode -- the opposite profile from cognitive reappraisal, which is applied early and carries none of those costs.
terms.whyItMatters: When a Human Resources Management Series judge asks how you would hold composure while an employee vents about a denied raise, an answer built on hiding what you felt names the strategy research links to worse recall of the conversation; the scoring answer reinterprets the outburst before it peaks.

terms.definition: Groups buyers by what they measurably did — purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty status, benefit sought — read from transaction records, while psychographic segmentation groups them by what they say they value and geographic segmentation by where they live; a heavy user and a light user can match on every demographic and psychographic trait and still belong in different behavioral segments, so it is the only base that predicts volume directly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty-program roleplays ask which customers to reward; the winning answer segments on measured usage rate rather than on who the customers are.

terms.definition: Forbids a director, officer, partner or agent from self-dealing, taking an opportunity that belonged to the enterprise, or competing with the principal, and a challenged transaction is judged on whether it was entirely fair rather than whether it was well reasoned. That standard is the split from the duty of care, where the business judgment rule shields an informed, disinterested, good-faith decision even when it turns out badly.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics roleplays about a manager steering a supply contract to a relative's firm are loyalty problems, not care problems.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: Launching into a different product category under an existing brand name — Dove soap into Dove shampoo — whereas a line extension adds a variant inside the category the brand already sells, such as another Dove soap scent; the category jump risks diluting what the parent name means, while the in-category variant mainly risks stealing volume from its own siblings, so the two carry different failure modes and different tests.
terms.whyItMatters: Product roleplays that hand you a growth mandate are scored on naming which of the two you chose and the specific risk it carries; treating them as the same move loses both points.

terms.definition: A court's decision to set aside limited liability and reach the owners' personal assets, available when the entity was run as a mere alter ego: personal and business funds commingled, formalities ignored, the firm deliberately undercapitalized at formation, or the corporate form used to work a fraud. Ordinary business failure never suffices — the owner has to have treated the corporation as a pocketbook.
terms.whyItMatters: Ownership-structure roleplays ask what an entrepreneur must actually do after incorporating to keep a house and savings out of reach.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: Share of respondents who name a brand when asked only to list the brands they can think of in a category with nothing shown to them, as opposed to aided awareness, where the interviewer reads the name and the respondent only confirms recognition; aided scores typically run two to four times higher than unaided ones, so the two measures can never be compared with each other or with a competitor's differently-worded question.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand you awareness research want you to challenge the number's basis before acting on it; treating an aided figure as proof of strong awareness is the standard trap.

terms.definition: The default American rule that either side may end the relationship at any time for any reason or none, narrowed by three recognized exceptions: a public-policy exception covering firing for jury service, refusing to break the law, or whistleblowing; an implied-contract exception built from handbook language or long practice; and, in a minority of states, an implied covenant of good faith. Statutes on race, sex, age, disability and retaliation override it outright.
terms.whyItMatters: Termination roleplays ask what a manager may put in a handbook without accidentally promising contractual job security.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: A federal tax election under Subchapter S that keeps corporate limited liability while passing profit and loss straight through to the owners' personal returns, escaping the double taxation a C corporation pays once at the entity level and again on dividends. The price is eligibility: no more than 100 shareholders, only individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, and a single class of stock.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-ownership exam items ask which form a startup taking on 120 investors or a foreign backer can no longer use.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: Reaches single-firm conduct and requires two elements: monopoly power in a properly defined relevant market, and the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power through exclusionary conduct rather than growth from a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident. Section 1 instead needs an agreement between two or more parties restraining trade, so one firm acting alone can violate Section 2 and never Section 1.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-issues exam items about a dominant platform cutting off rivals turn on which section of the Act is even available.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Blocks a merger or acquisition whose effect may be substantially to lessen competition — an incipiency standard reaching a deal before any harm has occurred, unlike the Sherman Act, which needs a completed restraint or actual monopolization. Deals above reporting thresholds must be cleared with the FTC and DOJ before closing, and the agencies may sue to enjoin, force divestiture, or accept behavioral conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Merger roleplays ask why regulators can stop a deal that has not yet raised a single price for a single customer.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: The classification system that assigns every imported article a code — six digits harmonized worldwide, extended to ten digits in the United States — and it is that code, not the invoice description, which sets the duty rate and any quota or trade-remedy exposure. Misclassification remains the importer's liability even when a customs broker filed the entry, so back duties and negligence penalties land on the buyer.
terms.whyItMatters: Customs-regulation roleplays ask why two nearly identical shirts arrive carrying very different duty rates.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Bans unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce, and the deception branch is a three-part test: a representation, omission or practice, likely to mislead a consumer acting reasonably under the circumstances, that is material to the purchase decision. The unfairness branch is separate — substantial consumer injury that is not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits — and neither branch requires proving the seller intended to mislead anyone.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion roleplays about an ad whose fine print reverses the headline are scored on materiality and the reasonable-consumer standard, not on intent.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: A defense to copyright infringement weighed on the four statutory factors of 17 U.S.C. section 107: the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is transformative or commercial; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and substantiality of the portion taken; and the effect on the potential market for the original. No factor is decisive and there is no safe word count or percentage, though the market-effect factor usually carries the most weight.
terms.whyItMatters: IP-protection roleplays about quoting a rival's review or reusing its product photo in a comparison ad are argued factor by factor.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.
